# Introduction

Alzheimer's disease (AD) and frontotemporal dementia (FTD) are both cortical
neurodegenerative diseases, but their atrophy follows very different spatial patterns. AD
involves the medial temporal lobe, the posterior cingulate/precuneus and lateral
temporoparietal cortex; behavioural-variant FTD involves orbitofrontal, anterior cingulate
and anterior insular cortex; the language variants of FTD are left-lateralised, in the
anterior temporal lobe (semantic variant) or the posterior frontal and insular cortex
(non-fluent variant). The network-degeneration hypothesis proposes that these patterns are
shaped by the brain's connectivity: atrophy maps resemble intrinsic connectivity networks
[1], regions connected to an epicentre are more affected [2, 5], and network spreading
models reproduce group and individual patterns [3, 6, 7, 10].

Two methodological issues limit how much these findings say about networks. First, atrophy
maps and connectomes are both spatially smooth and both organised by distance: nearby
regions tend to be connected and tend to have similar atrophy. A network model can therefore
predict atrophy well simply because connections are short [13, 23]. Few studies compare
network models with a purely spatial model that has the same freedom [8, 9, 11]. Second,
the null models used to test network effects differ in what they preserve. Spatial
permutation ("spin") tests preserve the map's spatial autocorrelation only approximately
[19], and degree-preserving rewiring of the connectome destroys its geometry, so that almost
any spatially smooth map looks network-constrained.

The structural connectome supports many candidate routes of communication, from direct
connections and shortest paths to diffusion, search-information and navigation models
[12–15]. Which of these, if any, best explains atrophy, and whether the answer differs
between diseases with different spatial patterns, has not been tested. Here we compared these
communication models, functional connectivity and generative spreading models with Euclidean
and along-the-cortex (geodesic) spatial baselines, in AD, MCI and the FTD syndromes, using
openly shared atrophy maps, cortical and subcortical parcellations registered to the
templates of the maps, and five null models with all parameters refitted inside every null.
We asked three questions: does any network model explain atrophy beyond spatial proximity;
is the answer different for AD and FTD; and how much do conclusions depend on the null
model.
